identity.description:
Add the consumer workflow so the reviewer runs on this repo

The repo ships the reusable workflow but had no workflow of its own, so its pull requests got no review. This PR adds `.github/workflows/pr-review.yml`, the file the README's "Set up CI" section tells a consumer to save.

A test in `test/packaging.test.ts` keeps the file equal to the README snippet and checks that the snippet calls a workflow this repo holds.

This PR is the first run of the reviewer on this repo.

file_notes.note: New consumer workflow. Uses privileged triggers (pull_request_target, issue_comment), write permissions, secrets inherited, and a tag-pinned reusable workflow. Check that fork PRs and comment authors cannot abuse it.

New tests. One checks the workflow file equals the README yaml snippet. One checks the reusable workflow path exists in the repo. The snippet parsing breaks if the README heading or code fence is missing, and the path check depends on how the `uses` string is stripped.

triage.summary: Adds a GitHub Actions workflow that runs the PR review reusable workflow on pull request, label, and comment events, with write permissions and inherited secrets. Adds packaging tests that check the file matches the README snippet and that the referenced reusable workflow exists locally. The security posture of the triggers and permissions is the main concern.

findings.claim: The description says this PR is the first run of the reviewer on this repo, but the workflow calls the reviewer at the `@v1` tag. So the run uses the released v1 code, not the code at the head of this PR.
findings.suggested_fix: Say in the description that the run uses the `v1` release, or make sure the `v1` tag exists.

findings.claim: readmeSnippet does not check that indexOf finds the heading or the fence, so a missing marker silently selects the wrong text.
findings.evidence: const section = readme.slice(readme.indexOf("### The consumer workflow"));
findings.suggested_fix: Assert that each indexOf result is not -1 before you slice.
findings.explanation: indexOf returns -1 on a miss, and slice(-1) or a start of 7 yields an unrelated substring.

findings.claim: readmeSnippet does not check indexOf results, so a missing heading or fence makes it slice the wrong text instead of failing clearly.
findings.suggested_fix: Assert that each indexOf result is not -1 before you slice.

findings.claim: pull_request_target and issue_comment triggers run with base-repo secrets and write tokens on events from untrusted forks or commenters, and secrets: inherit passes all secrets to the called workflow.
findings.suggested_fix: Pass only the needed secrets explicitly, and make sure the reusable workflow gates on author association and never executes PR head code.
findings.explanation: Privileged triggers combined with inherited secrets and write permissions expose secrets if the reusable workflow checks out or processes PR head content.

findings.claim: The job grants contents: write, which a review job probably does not need.
findings.suggested_fix: Use contents: read unless a write is required.
findings.explanation: Wider token permissions than needed increase the damage if the workflow is compromised.

findings.claim: The reusable workflow is pinned to a mutable tag while it receives inherited secrets.
findings.explanation: A moved tag changes the code that runs with secrets and does not change this file.

findings.claim: The pull_request_target and issue_comment triggers run with base-repo secrets inherited and write permissions, so fork PRs or any commenter can start a privileged run.
findings.suggested_fix: Make sure review.yml checks author_association or a maintainer label, and pass only the secrets it needs instead of using `secrets: inherit`.
findings.explanation: These triggers run in the base repo context with secrets, so the called workflow must check the actor's authorization and must not run untrusted PR code.

findings.claim: The job grants contents: write, which a review job probably does not need.
findings.suggested_fix: Use contents: read unless the workflow really needs write access.
findings.explanation: A token with more scope than needed lets a compromised or prompt-injected run push to the repo.

findings.claim: The reusable workflow is pinned to the mutable tag @v1 and gets all secrets through secrets: inherit.
findings.suggested_fix: Pin to a commit SHA, or use a local `./.github/workflows/review.yml` reference, and pass secrets explicitly.
findings.explanation: Anyone who can move the v1 tag can change the code that runs with every repo secret.

first.rationale: The reusable workflow already gates pull_request_target on a maintainer-applied review: label and issue_comment on author association, and it treats the PR checkout as data. The finding is generic speculation; the setup matches the documented design, with at most a minor hardening point on secrets: inherit.

#   another script or build from the workspace.
escalated.rationale: The called workflow already does what the suggested fix asks. It accepts a comment only from an OWNER, MEMBER or COLLABORATOR. A pull_request_target run needs a "review:" label, which only a user with triage permission can add. The PR checkout is treated as data and never run, and persist-credentials is false. The finding is a speculative "if" that the code already guards against, and narrowing `secrets: inherit` would only harden things a little.

first.rationale: The reusable workflow pushes review records to the `pr-review-records` branch, so `contents: write` is required. The README and the design doc say so, and the called workflow's own permissions block asks for it. A job that calls a reusable workflow can't pass on more than the caller grants, so lowering it to read would break the push.
